title: The JDK and the JVM
description: What happens between pressing Run and seeing output: compiling to bytecode, then running it.

content.value: When you press Run, your code does not go straight to the computer. It is first **compiled** (checked and translated), then **executed** (run).

steps.label: Main.java
steps.detail: your code, text you can read

steps.label: Output
steps.detail: what you see in the terminal

content.title: What happens when you press Run
content.caption: If `javac` finds a mistake, it stops and tells you. The JVM step never happens.
Even this one line goes through both steps.

content.question: You forget a semicolon and press Run. What happens?
options: `javac` stops with an error, and nothing runs
The program runs and skips that line
The JVM adds the semicolon for you
It runs, then crashes at the end
content.explain: Compiling is a checking step. A mistake there means step two, running, never happens.

items.sub: What `javac` makes: instructions for an imaginary computer, not for your exact machine.
A real program that pretends to be that imaginary computer.
There is a JVM for Windows, Mac, Linux and Android.

content.real: A game disc that plays on any console of the right kind
content.concept: Bytecode that runs on any JVM
content.text: This is the trick behind "write once, run anywhere". Compile on a laptop, run on a server, no changes needed.

content.question: Which file do **you** write?
options: `Main.class`
The JVM
`Main.java`
`javac`
content.explain: You write the `.java` file (source code). `javac` writes the `.class` file (bytecode) for you.

content.text: Three names that sound alike. Each one contains the one before it, plus a little more.

items.sub: The JVM plus the **standard library**: ready-made code that comes with Java.
The JRE plus developer tools, including the `javac` compiler.

content.value: To **run** Java you need the JRE. To **write** Java you need the JDK, because only it can compile. Here, the JDK is already installed on the server for you.

content.caption: `System.out.println` comes from the standard library in the JRE.

practice.question: Write a program that prints the two steps in order: one line saying Step 1: compile, and one saying Step 2: run.

quiz.question: What does `javac` do?
options: Checks your code and translates it into bytecode.
Runs your program and shows the output.
Installs Java on your computer.
quiz.explain: `javac` is the compiler. It reads your `.java` file, reports any mistakes, and writes a `.class` file of bytecode.

quiz.question: What runs the bytecode?
options: The JVM, the Java Virtual Machine.
The compiler.
The text editor.
quiz.explain: The JVM is the engine that executes bytecode. Because every operating system has its own JVM, the same bytecode runs on all of them.

quiz.question: You want to write and compile Java programs. Which do you need installed?
options: The JDK, because only it includes the compiler.
The JRE, because it includes everything.
Only the JVM.
quiz.explain: The JRE can run a finished program but cannot compile one. The JDK adds `javac`, so a developer needs the JDK.

quiz.question: Why can the same Java program run on Windows, Mac and Android?
options: Bytecode targets the JVM, and each system has its own JVM.
Java rewrites itself for each machine as it runs.
It cannot: you have to write it again for each system.
quiz.explain: Your code is compiled for the JVM rather than for a specific machine. Each system supplies a JVM that knows how to run that bytecode.
